text: The last three lessons covered what's genuinely new about AI security — natural language as a command channel, non-deterministic output, training data and model weights as assets, the real OWASP categories, and NIST's four functions. None of that erases the disciplines you've already built. This lesson closes the chapter by showing exactly how each one still does real work, and where the new layer attaches to it.

Every LLM feature is, underneath, an API call, so authentication, authorization, rate-limiting, and logging all still apply in full. What's new is what that call contains: the prompt is attacker-reachable natural language, which is Prompt Injection, and the response needs the same untrusted-input treatment on the way out, which is Insecure Output Handling. Data classification extends the same way — it now has to cover whatever data goes into training or fine-tuning, and whatever a retrieval system feeds into the model's context, because sensitive data in either one can resurface as Sensitive Information Disclosure or bypass access control you already enforce elsewhere.

Supply chain security gets a parallel track: foundation models, fine-tuned checkpoints, datasets, and plugins pulled from public hubs each carry their own provenance question, the same way a third-party package does — who built it, on what data, with what known weaknesses. And identity and access control matters more, not less, once agents can take real actions. An agent should hold only the permissions its task requires, scoped and time-limited like any other service account, because Excessive Agency is exactly what happens when that discipline gets skipped.

The pattern repeats across all four: the fundamental practice stays the discipline you already know, and the new work is scoping it to cover an additional surface — the prompt and response payload, the training and retrieval pipeline, the model and plugin supply chain, the agent's own credentials.

That's the practical takeaway for this whole chapter: AI security engineering is mostly your existing disciplines applied to a new kind of component, plus a focused set of genuinely new concerns on top. Chapter 2 picks up the first of those in depth — prompt injection, and how to actually defend against it.
